fields.title: Mayak: Launch Delayed by Four Weeks
fields.summary: The status was green for a month. The status email goes out tomorrow morning. Decide what to say and to whom.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do today, and what will you write in tomorrow's email?
fields.brief/role: You are the product manager for the team building the client portal.
fields.brief/company: Mayak is a fictional 90-person company that sells a case management system to law firms.
fields.brief/context: The portal was scheduled to launch in two weeks. This morning, the team confirmed: work on authentication, discovered during testing, adds about four weeks, making the launch six weeks away. Three clients were given the original date; one scheduled internal training for the launch week. Your manager reported a green status to leadership for a month based on your updates. The weekly status email goes out tomorrow morning.
fields.brief/objective: Communicate the shift to maintain trust without disrupting client plans.
fields.brief/constraints: The four-week estimate comes from the tech lead, with a range of three to five weeks. It cannot be compressed without dropping the activity log, which two of the three clients require.
fields.brief/task: Decide what you will do today and what will go into the email.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Bad news is delivered early and in the right order
fields.learnTakeaway/body: Waiting for certainty is the most common way to turn a delay into a scandal. People around you have their own deadlines that arrive before your certainty. A range with an update date is a normal message; silence when a problem is known is not. The order is usually the same: the person who shouldn't hear it from others first, then the person with the closest deadline, then everyone else.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
From a conversation with the tech lead:

"The portal needs to let in people who are not our clients' employees—their clients. We planned to reuse the employee account system. Testing revealed it gives implicit access to case details that external users must not see. This means we need a separate login path with its own permissions model.

Four weeks is my estimate. Three if the permissions model turns out as simple as I think, five if not. I can give a precise date in a week, once we break down permissions by role."

The activity log cannot be removed: without it, their own security team won't approve external access.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Olkhin & Partners: scheduled internal training for launch week, 40 people, contracted trainer. Canceling more than three weeks in advance costs nothing; closer than that, they pay a fee.

Desvik: mentioned no dependencies. Their account manager asks for a written monthly update and is generally relaxed.

Marchmont: told their largest client that the portal would be available "this quarter." Six weeks fits tightly into the quarter.

Account Manager: "Trust after last time is average. I should call Olkhin, but with you on the line."
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Your manager in a 1-on-1 meeting two months ago: "I don't mind bad news. I mind finding out from someone else, and hearing about a problem when it's already unfixable."

The previous product manager for this product pushed back the launch twice, announcing it about a week before the original date both times. The second time, the client escalated to the CEO.

The procedure for bad news is not documented anywhere: who speaks first, how far in advance, and in what format—everyone decides for themselves.

The weekly status email is read by 40 people, including two board members.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Tech lead: "I can give an exact date in a week. Right now, it's a range."

Account manager: "Olkhin should know before the training cancellation deadline. That's in three days."

Commercial Director (found out by chance): "Just don't write 'red' in the email the board reads until we know the exact date."

Your manager: on vacation until Thursday, reachable by phone.

Lawyer: pilot contracts have no fixed dates, only an "estimated timeframe"; no penalties for delays.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Announce immediately with a range and clarification date
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Call your manager today, mark the status red in the email with a reason, contact Olkhin before the training cancellation deadline, and promise an exact date in a week.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
Your manager learns from you over the phone, not from the email—exactly what they asked for two months ago.
Olkhin & Partners cancel the training three days before the deadline and pay no fee. Their admin says it is the first time they were warned in advance.
The email shows a red status, the reason in two sentences, a three-to-five-week range, and a date when a precise estimate will be ready. The board sees this as a controlled situation because the next update date is clear.
You call Marchmont yourself: six weeks fits into their quarter, and they need to hear this before promising anything else to their client.
In a week, the four-week estimate is confirmed, and this is now a second update, not a surprise.
Trade-off: the commercial director was unhappy about the red status in an email the board reads, which required a separate conversation.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: Keep your manager from finding out via email, but wait a week to give clients a single firm date.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
Your manager is warned, which is half the job—the internal half.
The second half costs the client money: Olkhin's training cancellation deadline passes in three days, and you talk to them in a week. Forty people, a contracted trainer, and a late cancellation fee.
When you finally call, the conversation isn't about the delay, but about why you knew and stayed silent.
The account manager explicitly warned you about this deadline.
Trade-off: internal trust preserved, external trust burned—even though you could have shared a range immediately and provided an exact date later.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Drop the activity log and delay by three weeks
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Remove the log, reduce the delay to three weeks, and present this as the plan.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Three weeks instead of six sounds better, and it's met with relief at the meeting.
Until the first talk with clients: two out of three require the log, and without it, their security team won't approve external access at all.
So the portal launches three weeks earlier, but cannot be turned on for two out of three pilot clients.
A month later, the log gets built anyway—only now after a public promise.
Trade-off: timeline improved by sacrificing the core reason the product was bought, which would have been revealed in the very first client call.
fields.decisionOptions/3/label: Wait a week for an exact estimate
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: Keep status yellow, say nothing outside the team for now, and communicate one firm date in eight days.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
In eight days, you do have an exact date—four weeks.
By then, the training cancellation deadline has passed, Olkhin & Partners pay a fee, and your manager learns about the problem at the same time they learn the team knew about it a week ago.
The previous PM announced delays a week before the deadline twice, and the second time the client went to the CEO; people remember this.
A yellow status in an email read by two board members, despite a known four-week delay, is what will later be called a cover-up.
Trade-off: gained accuracy nobody asked for, at the cost of the single thing asked for—advance warning.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Acquisition plan relies on a single channel without reserve or capacity knowledge
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Retention reduced to mechanics instead of processes with an owner and metric
fields.rubric/remediation/2/gap: Launch reduced to an announcement date without decisions on segment, promise, and success
fields.rubric/remediation/3/gap: Business unit closure lacks a plan for offboarding people and data
fields.rubric/remediation/4/gap: External communication evaluated by incoming requests and unprepared for bad news
